title: All, Every and Whole: Totality and Frequency
summary: Distinguish everyone/everything from all, express complete quantities and entire objects using all or whole, and contrast repeated occasions (every day, every time) with continuous periods (all day, all the time). Use singular verbs with every/everyone while allowing singular they to refer back to people.
learningObjectives: Choose everyone or everything for general statements and all in the appropriate noun, pronoun and relative-clause patterns.
Use the whole before a complete singular countable item, but all before uncountable quantities.
Distinguish every day/every time from all day/all the time in context.
Use singular agreement after every, everyone, everybody and everything, and natural singular-they reference.

explanation.heading: Everyone and everything as subjects or objects
explanation.body: Everyone or everybody refers to all the people in a relevant group; everything refers to all the things or events. In ordinary complete statements, choose everyone enjoyed the event or everything went smoothly rather than using bare all for the same meaning. All normally needs a noun (all customers), an of-phrase (all of them), a position after a subject (they all agreed), or a following clause (all I need).
explanation.example: Everyone received a programme, and everything started on schedule.

explanation.heading: All in several useful structures
explanation.body: All + noun describes a complete group or quantity: all passengers and all the advice. Use all of before an object pronoun: all of us, all of you, all of them. All can also follow the subject before the main verb or after a form of be: they all laughed, they were all ready. All + a clause can mean the only thing or things: All I need is a quiet place. All about means detailed knowledge of a topic.
explanation.example: All of us were exhausted, but we all stayed until the end.

explanation.heading: Whole means an entire singular item or period
explanation.body: Whole describes one complete object or a complete period, rather than only a part. A determiner such as the, a, this or my usually appears before whole: the whole report, a whole afternoon, my whole career. Whole normally modifies singular countable nouns, not uncountable nouns such as equipment, money, furniture or information. Use all the information rather than the whole information.
explanation.example: We listened to the whole recording before discussing the details.

explanation.heading: Every for repeated events; all for continuous duration
explanation.body: Every + singular countable time noun expresses how frequently an event occurs: every afternoon, every three weeks or every ten minutes. All day or the whole day refers to the entire duration of one day; the same distinction applies to all morning and the whole evening. Standard idiomatic wording is all day, not all the day. Every day describes repetition across different days, not continuous duration during one day.
explanation.example: The security team checks the doors every hour but watches the entrance all night.

explanation.heading: Every time versus all the time, and singular agreement
explanation.body: Every time means on each occasion an event happens; all the time means continuously or very frequently throughout a period. Every, everyone, everybody and everything are grammatically singular, so use a singular verb: every ticket has a number; everybody is ready. To refer back to everyone or everybody, singular they/their/them is common and natural: everyone brought their ID.
explanation.example: Every time the signal drops, everyone checks their connection.

comparisons.title: An entire item versus all of a quantity

left.label: Whole + singular countable noun
left.note: The document is one countable item and was checked from beginning to end.

right.label: All + uncountable noun
right.note: Information is uncountable, so whole is not the usual modifier.

left.label: Every day: repeated occasions
left.example: The team meets every day this week.
left.note: One meeting occurs on each day in the stated period.

right.label: All day: one continuous period
right.example: The team worked all day on Tuesday.

left.label: Every time: separate occasions
left.example: Every time the lift stops, the light turns red.
left.note: The red light appears on each separate occasion.

right.label: All the time: continuous state
right.example: The light stays red all the time.
right.note: The light remains red continuously, rather than only when the lift stops.

examples.sentence: Everything in the parcel was wrapped securely.
examples.note: Everything is a singular subject referring to all the contents.

examples.sentence: All I want is a clear explanation of the delay.
examples.note: All + a following clause means the only thing wanted.

examples.sentence: The whole neighbourhood lost electricity for an hour.
examples.note: The whole describes an entire identifiable neighbourhood.

examples.sentence: She read all the information before signing the form.
examples.note: Information is uncountable and naturally takes all, not whole.

examples.sentence: The guard checks the side door every twenty minutes.
examples.note: Every + a time interval specifies a repeated schedule.

examples.sentence: Everyone showed their ticket before entering.
examples.note: Everyone takes a singular verb; their can refer back to people of any gender.

commonMistakes.why: For a general statement about all the people present, everyone is more natural than bare all.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We reviewed the whole equipment before the inspection.
commonMistakes.correct: We reviewed all the equipment before the inspection.
commonMistakes.why: Equipment is uncountable, so use all the equipment rather than the whole equipment.

commonMistakes.incorrect: She has checked her email all days this week.
commonMistakes.correct: She has checked her email every day this week.
commonMistakes.why: Every day describes repeated daily occasions; all days is not the normal time expression here.
Everybody is grammatically singular, requiring has; their is natural as a singular-they reference.

studyTips: Draw two timelines: several distinct ticks for every day and one continuous bar for all day. Build one sentence for each timeline.
Before whole, check whether the noun is a single countable item and whether a determiner such as the or my is present.
Underline everyone, everybody, everything and every + noun in your writing, then check the verb is singular even when their refers back to people.

exercises.prompt: The instructions were clear, and ___ understood what to do.
exercises.feedback: Everyone is a natural singular pronoun meaning all the people involved.

exercises.prompt: The analyst examined ___ before presenting the findings. The report included every measurement.
exercises.feedback: Data is treated here as an uncountable mass noun, so all the data is the natural phrase.

exercises.prompt: The bus arrives once every fifteen minutes. It arrives ___ .
exercises.feedback: Every fifteen minutes describes a recurring interval rather than continuous duration.

exercises.prompt: We worked from nine in the morning until six in the evening without stopping. We worked ___ .
exercises.feedback: All day describes continuous activity over a complete day.

exercises.prompt: The manager read ___ report, from the first page to the last. (two words meaning the complete singular report)
exercises.feedback: The whole + singular countable report describes the complete document.

exercises.prompt: The alarm sounds ___ time the door is opened without a pass. (one word meaning on each occasion)
exercises.feedback: Every time introduces a repeated condition.

exercises.prompt: ___ in the department has received their new access card. (one singular subject pronoun for all the people)
exercises.feedback: Everyone acts as a singular subject and may be followed by their.

exercises.prompt: The computers are switched on ___ the time during the test. (one word meaning continuously)
exercises.feedback: All the time describes continuous operation throughout the test.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Everything in these boxes are fragile.
acceptedAnswers: Everything in these boxes is fragile.
exercises.feedback: Everything is grammatically singular, so use is rather than are.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: We read the whole information carefully before approving the plan.
acceptedAnswers: We read all the information carefully before approving the plan.
exercises.feedback: Information is uncountable, so all the information is idiomatic and whole information is not.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The maintenance worker checks the system all day at 8 a.m.
acceptedAnswers: The maintenance worker checks the system every day at 8 a.m.
exercises.feedback: A scheduled check at 8 a.m. happens once on each day, so use every day rather than all day.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: She completed whole assignment before lunch.
acceptedAnswers: She completed the whole assignment before lunch.
exercises.feedback: Whole normally needs a determiner such as the before a specific singular countable noun.

speakingExercises.prompt: Use the facts: every person in the group; receive; a badge. Say one sentence starting with “Everyone”, using the past simple and ending with “a badge”.
speakingExercises.feedback: Everyone means all the people considered and takes a singular verb.

speakingExercises.prompt: Rephrase “I read the report from beginning to end.” as one complete sentence. Begin with “I read” and use “the whole report”.
speakingExercises.feedback: The whole report describes one complete countable document.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say one sentence with these facts: the clinic; open; every Saturday. Use the present simple and begin with “The clinic”.
speakingExercises.feedback: Every Saturday describes a regular weekly event.

speakingExercises.prompt: A colleague asks whether you left the meeting early. You stayed from start to finish. Respond with one sentence beginning “I stayed”, using “the whole meeting” and no other details.
acceptedAnswers: I stayed for the whole meeting.
speakingExercises.feedback: The whole meeting means the entire duration of that one event.

speakingExercises.prompt: Make this sentence natural by replacing the incorrect quantity phrase, but change nothing else: “They checked the whole equipment.”
speakingExercises.feedback: Equipment is uncountable, so all the equipment is the correct phrase.

speakingExercises.prompt: Describe a constant noise in one sentence. Use exactly: “The alarm”, “rings”, and “all the time”, in that order.
acceptedAnswers: The alarm rings all the time.
speakingExercises.feedback: All the time expresses something continuous or very frequent.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences, in this order. Facts: everyone / be / ready, present simple; they / all / have / tickets, present simple. Start with “Everyone” and then “They”.
acceptedAnswers: Everyone is ready. They all have tickets.
speakingExercises.feedback: Everyone takes is; they all is another way to refer to the complete group.

speakingExercises.prompt: A printer jams on each occasion when a large file is sent. Begin with “Every time”, use “we send a large file” and then say “the printer jams”.
acceptedAnswers: Every time we send a large file, the printer jams.
speakingExercises.feedback: Every time introduces the repeated condition that triggers the same result.

listeningExercises.audioText: The museum opens every Friday evening, but it does not remain open all night.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker say about Friday evenings?
choices: The museum is open continuously through the night.
It opens regularly on Fridays, for only part of the evening or night.
It opens on one Friday per year.
listeningExercises.feedback: Every Friday describes a repeated opening; not all night limits its duration.

listeningExercises.audioText: The entire production team stayed for the whole rehearsal, from the first scene to the final note.
listeningExercises.prompt: How much of the rehearsal did the team attend?
listeningExercises.feedback: The whole rehearsal and the described start and finish indicate full attendance.

listeningExercises.audioText: Everyone in the room has been told about the change of venue.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the single subject word immediately before “in the room”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Everyone refers to all the people and takes singular agreement.

listeningExercises.audioText: I only check my messages once a day, but my colleague looks at the screen all the time.
listeningExercises.prompt: How do the two habits differ?
choices: The speaker checks once daily; the colleague checks continually.
Both check their messages only once a week.
listeningExercises.feedback: Once a day indicates daily repetition; all the time expresses near-continuous attention.

listeningExercises.audioText: We have been collecting records for months, and everything is now organised by date.
listeningExercises.prompt: What is the current state of the collected records?
choices: Only the oldest record has been organised.
The entire collection is arranged by date.
listeningExercises.feedback: Everything is organised means no part of the relevant collection has been left unarranged.

listeningExercises.audioText: Every time the detector senses movement, a small green light flashes for two seconds.
listeningExercises.prompt: When does the green light flash?
choices: On each occasion that movement is detected.
Only once when the detector is installed.
listeningExercises.feedback: Every time links the brief flash to each occurrence of detected movement.

listeningExercises.audioText: We spent all day sorting the donated clothes into labelled boxes.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word duration expression immediately after “spent”.
listeningExercises.feedback: All day describes work continuing throughout one day.

listeningExercises.audioText: I read the whole manual before attempting the repair myself.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word expression immediately before “manual”.
listeningExercises.feedback: The whole manual means the entire single document, not just sections.
